1:
The opening verse turns on who is meant by the man of reproofs. John Gill offers both: a man who censures others while doing the same things, and so needs an impudent face and a brow of brass; or, as he prefers, a man often reproved by others. Keil and Delitzsch grant that the first is the impression the phrase makes at once, but set it aside on grammar: the noun after man elsewhere in this book names what proceeds from the subject, not what he does to others. Matthew Henry lists the reprovers — parents and friends, magistrates and ministers, providence and conscience — and observes that some will not give the reproof a hearing, while others hear it and go on in the sin. Charles Ellicott makes the hardened neck a refusal to bear the easy yoke, and presses the closing words: the man is not destroyed merely but shattered, like a potter's vessel that cannot be mended, no remedy being left for one who has despised God's warnings.

Henry treats the proverb on rulers as a repetition: the people both have cause to rejoice or mourn and actually do so, as their rulers are righteous or wicked. On the son who loves wisdom he makes an etymological point: such a man is properly a philosopher, that word meaning a lover of wisdom, and religion being the best philosophy. Ellicott sends the reader to the parable of the prodigal for the second clause; Clarke, rendering it that he who feeds harlots utterly destroys his substance, asks whether there has ever been a single case to the contrary.

What ruins a land under a king is disputed. Our version and most voices read bribery, Ellicott glossing the gifts as taken to pervert justice and John Wesley calling them bribes. Clarke supplies a national instance: the selling of justice was notorious in England before the great charter, whose article promising that justice would be sold to none was framed against it, and he has met with cases in the records where a man nearly ruined himself in presents to the king, the queen and their favourites to have his case decided in his favour. Delitzsch alone translates otherwise, making the ruinous figure a man of taxes rather than a taker of bribes, so the second line describes exaction rather than corruption.

On the flatterer the disagreement concerns intention. Henry has him commending good which is absent or not what it is represented to be, and doing it with an ill design, since he would not praise as he does but for what he hopes to get; hence his rule that it is wisdom to suspect flatterers. Delitzsch rejects two scholars who translate the verse as circumventing a neighbour with flatteries, pointing out that the preposition carries no hostile intention and that the effect follows whether the flatterer means it or not: the web he weaves before his neighbour's eyes becomes a net when the man is caught in it.

On the snare in transgression Gill records that the accents in some copies allow a different division, an evil snare rather than an evil man, and Delitzsch works through the same accentuation; Henry makes the sin its own punishment, the transgressor held in the cords of his own iniquity; Ellicott has the wicked man ignorant of how repentance might let him escape, and the righteous rejoicing because his conscience is clear. On the cause of the poor Gill enters a caution none of the others make: the poor man's person is not to be favoured in judgment any more than the rich man's, an affectation of mercy being as much a perversion as partiality the other way. What is considered is the cause. Ellicott gives the contrast a face: the wicked man cares as little for his poorer neighbour as Dives did for the beggar at his own door.
8:
Matthew Henry draws the fullest portrait of the scornful men who endanger a city, every clause turning on the scorn: they act precipitately because they scorn to deliberate, illegally because they scorn to be hampered by laws, break faith because they scorn to be bound by their word, and provoke the people because they scorn to please them. The verb is disputed. Our version has them bringing a city into a snare, but John Gill reports the Greek and Syriac reading that they burn it; Keil and Delitzsch agree the word means to blow, not to ensnare, so the inhabitants are stirred until they burn; Charles Ellicott renders it to fan the passions, the wise allaying anger by gentle counsels.

Who rages and laughs in the next verse is a genuine crux. Delitzsch reports that Jerome and Luther made the wise man the subject throughout — whether he is angry or laughs, he finds no rest — and that later scholars followed; his own rendering gives the raging and laughing to the fool. Ellicott sets out both without choosing; Adam Clarke quotes Coverdale, who keeps the first sense — a wise man going to law with a fool gets no rest, deal he gently or roughly. Henry states the upshot: contending with a wise man he may hope to be understood, but with a fool he will see no end of it.

At the verse on bloody men Delitzsch declines the nearest translation: reading that the upright seek the guiltless man's life is possible, but the contrast forbids it, so he makes the men of blood the subject of both clauses. Ellicott keeps the received division and turns the second clause into active charity, the just caring for the life of the perfect man — which John Wesley puts in two words, to preserve it. Henry adds that bloody men especially grudge upright magistrates, who would restrain them.

What the fool pours out is disputed on the same grounds. Delitzsch argues that the noun is not spirit in the sense of what a man has in mind, but passionate emotion, since the contrasting verb means not to restrain but to hush up; Gill notes that the Targum and three ancient versions read wrath, and Ellicott gives both. Clarke turns the verse into counsel of another sort: a man should never deliver his whole mind while other opinions are still to come, since if he speaks again he must go over old ground. Henry describes the fault rather than the noun: the man who has in his mouth whatever is in his thoughts.

On the ruler who listens to lies, Clarke supplies the sharpest note in the chapter: wherever a system of espionage prevails a system of falsity is established with it, since a man capable of being a spy is capable of cutting his king's or his father's throat — and he has seen the same spy take pay from both parties and deceive both. Henry judges the ruler as severely as the liar, the receiver being as bad as the thief.

The pairing of the poor man with his opposite draws a survey from Clarke, who calls the second word hard to fix and lists what the versions made of it — the usurer, the creditor, the lender, the rich, the oppressors — before settling for the parallel proverb's sense. Delitzsch reads the usurer; Ellicott prefers the oppressor, finding in the lightening of both men's eyes a word to each: the one's sorrows will end, the other will meet stern vengeance. At the last verse Henry states what faithful judgment of the poor excludes as well as requires: they are not to be countenanced in an unjust cause for their poverty's sake, but neither may their poverty prejudice a just one. Gill sees Solomon here and the Messiah behind him.
15:
On the rod and reproof, Matthew Henry insists the two belong together in a fixed order: if a reproof will serve without the rod it is well, but the rod must never be used without a grave reproof beside it. He backs the promise with a Latin tag, that vexation sharpens the intellect. Charles Ellicott gives the neglected child a figure, left to wander unchecked like the wild ass, and lays the shame on the mother whose indulgence ruined him. John Gill turns the rod toward God's own children, who grow wiser under chastisement, and calls that man wise who hearkens to the rod and to him who appointed it.

The verse on multiplying wickedness gets very different treatment. Delitzsch judges it in the main a trivial saying, and reports the Swabian word for that kind of truism. Adam Clarke draws a doctrine of national judgment from it: wicked nations and families are cut off and rooted out, and were it not so righteousness would in time be banished from the earth — which he thinks accounts for many instances in which whole families fail. Henry describes the emboldening rather than the judgment: transgression grows more impudent when many keep it in countenance, as in the old world, where men degenerated as soon as they began to multiply.

On correcting a son, Henry describes a satisfaction none know but those who have it, of seeing the fruit of a good education and a prospect of a child's well-doing for both worlds.

The great verse of the chapter concerns vision, and the voices differ over both nouns. Gill and Wesley take the vision for prophecy in the sense of the public ministry of the word, and the verse as describing a want of men to administer it, instancing the days of Eli and Asa; Ellicott says the same, that God teaches none by his Spirit to instruct others. Delitzsch renders it revelation and marks the verse as important for judging how the wisdom writings stand to prophecy. On what happens to the people the versions pull apart: ours has them perish, Delitzsch has them become ungovernable, Ellicott run wild; Clarke quotes an old English Bible which followed the Vulgate in reading that the people shall be scattered, and states the rule that where divine revelation and faithful preaching are neither reverenced nor attended, the ruin of that land is not far off. Henry declines to choose, observing that the word has many significations and any will apply — the people are made naked, stripped of their ornaments and exposed to shame, or of their armour and exposed to danger.

The servant proverb is about the limits of speech. Ellicott is blunt that a slave must be corrected by sterner means, since only fear of punishment moves him, and reads the second clause as a refusal to answer a call or obey a command rather than an inability to understand; he sets the willing obedience of a son against the grudging obedience of a slave. Gill keeps the proverb to one kind of servant, since a well-disposed one needs only a word — bid to go, he goes — and it is the surly who must have blows; Wesley likewise makes the man a servant in the temper of his mind and not only in condition.

The closing verse compares two unpromising men, and both who take it up agree on the surprising order. Henry has more hope of making a scholar of a man dull and slow in his studies than of one with a mercurial genius who cannot fix, who gallops over a book and takes no time to digest it. Delitzsch puts it that the hasty man has blocked his own path to the wisdom which still stands open to the dull: the one is finished, of the other something may yet be made.
21:
The proverb on the pampered servant is obscure in its last word, and Keil and Delitzsch report how far the difficulty reaches: the Greek translators had no answer, and the Talmud resorted to an alphabet cipher to squeeze out a meaning. Charles Ellicott allows that confidential slaves sometimes did rise to be their master's heirs, but thinks the warning is against spoiling one by over-indulgence until he forgets his position, as old and petted servants grow dictatorial. Matthew Henry calls the indulgence imprudent, since the man is thereby spoiled for any other place; servants must endure hardness. Adam Clarke says such men forget their obligations and assume the rights of children; John Wesley expects him to grow insolent.

On the angry man the voices differ only in emphasis. Henry has him blowing the coals until he forces even those who would live quietly to fall out with him, and calls undue anger a sin causing many others.

Pride brings the same convergence, with one correction. John Gill takes the case back to Adam, who by affecting to be as God lost God's image and was brought to beggary and rags. Delitzsch describes the mechanism: the haughty man obscures the very honour he has by boasting of it immeasurably and aspiring after more. Ellicott corrects the second clause, which he would render not that honour upholds the lowly but that the lowly in spirit lay hold upon honour.

The partner of a thief draws careful legal comment. Ellicott identifies the cursing as the judge's adjuration that anyone with knowledge of the theft must give information, so the man who hears it and stays silent becomes an accomplice and shares the punishment. Clarke takes the hatred of his own soul for his life, which the outraged law may seize at any time. Delitzsch reports a rival construction making the first line the predicate of the second, so that the man who keeps another's guilty secret is declared no better than a thief's partner, and does not adopt it.

The fear of man is illustrated rather than defined. Henry supplies three instances at once — Abraham denying his wife, Peter his Master, and many a man his God and religion. Clarke turns it on the reader: where the mighty have been slain he will fall too unless he calls on the Strong for strength, and he must not be ashamed of Christ or his people or his cross. Gill distinguishes it from the fear of God, which leads to no snare, this being a servile fear with torment in it. Delitzsch reports a scholar's remark that a warning against the fear of man sounds strange in an eastern book, and answers by pointing to a prophet who gives the same warning.

The last two proverbs are about whose judgment counts. Clarke supposes the ruler's favour sought to escape the punishment the law has determined, and observes that a pardon so obtained does not take away guilt in God's sight. Ellicott says the same more broadly: the ruler's approval is of little value since God decides what each man is really worth. Henry notes that Solomon was himself a ruler and knew with what sedulity men applied to him, and calls it the way of the world to make interest with great men and expect much from the smiles of second causes. At the closing verse Henry finds not only the natural contrariety of virtue and vice, like light and darkness or fire and water, but the old enmity between the two seeds, and is careful that the sanctified bear good will to all souls while hating the practices of the impious. Clarke closes on a textual curiosity: the Latin version in some copies adds a line about the son who keeps the word not falling into perdition, which stood in the manuscript behind his own old English Bible.
